clinicalPearls: A leading cause of congenital visual impairment, characterised by an abnormally small optic disc with a reduced complement of retinal ganglion cell axons
The classic double-ring sign is a pale, small disc surrounded by a ring of pigment marking where the normal disc margin should lie
May be unilateral or bilateral; vision ranges from near normal to severe impairment, often with nystagmus in bilateral cases
Frequently associated with midline brain defects and hypopituitarism, forming part of septo-optic dysplasia
Endocrine assessment is essential because unrecognised cortisol or thyroid deficiency can be life-threatening in infancy
Neuroimaging with MRI evaluates the optic nerves, chiasm, septum pellucidum and pituitary
Risk factors include young maternal age and gestational exposures, though most cases are sporadic
reference.pathophysiology: Optic nerve hypoplasia results from a deficiency of retinal ganglion cell axons, arising either from failure of adequate axon generation or from excessive regression during development. Because optic nerve development is intimately linked with midline forebrain and hypothalamic-pituitary formation, the same developmental disturbance often produces associated midline brain malformations and pituitary dysfunction. The small disc has fewer nerve fibres, and the surrounding retinal pigment epithelium and lamina cribrosa create the double-ring appearance. Visual deficit reflects the degree of axonal deficiency, while the systemic consequences depend on the extent of hypothalamic-pituitary and midline involvement.
additionalDifferentials: Optic disc coloboma or morning glory anomaly
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain, orbits and pituitary region
Full endocrine evaluation including cortisol, thyroid, growth hormone and prolactin axes
OCT of the retinal nerve fibre layer where cooperation allows
redFlags: Neonatal hypoglycaemia or adrenal crisis from unrecognised hypopituitarism
Prolonged jaundice, micropenis or growth failure suggesting endocrine deficiency
Developmental regression or seizures suggesting broader brain malformation
Temperature instability pointing to hypothalamic dysfunction
reference.prognosis: Visual outcome varies widely from good to severely impaired and is generally stable, but overall prognosis and safety hinge on timely recognition and treatment of associated endocrine deficiencies.
pitfalls: Failing to arrange endocrine assessment and missing dangerous hormone deficiencies
Assuming unilateral disease excludes systemic associations
Overlooking the double-ring sign and misdiagnosing optic atrophy
Not imaging the brain to identify midline and pituitary anomalies
references: Taylor & Hoyt's Paediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
management: Undertake urgent endocrine evaluation and institute hormone replacement, including hydrocortisone for cortisol deficiency, levothyroxine for hypothyroidism and growth hormone, as unrecognised deficiency can be life-threatening in infancy
Image with MRI to define midline brain, chiasm, septum pellucidum and pituitary anomalies within the septo-optic dysplasia spectrum
Optimise vision with cycloplegic refraction, correction of refractive error and amblyopia management in unilateral cases
Provide low-vision aids and rehabilitation and manage associated nystagmus
Arrange developmental assessment and early intervention services
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across paediatric endocrinology, ophthalmology, neurology and developmental paediatrics
Offer genetic counselling where an underlying genetic cause is identified
